extraction.research_question: Can the perceived personality of public figures (Big Five traits and likability) be predicted from the location of their names in GPT-3's semantic embedding space, and does this hold after controlling for likability and demographics?
extraction.theory: Perceptions of others' personality are consequential and matter regardless of accuracy. Word embeddings act as a functional analogue of human semantic memory and encode word meanings, group stereotypes, and (per the authors) individual differences. The authors also invoke the personality halo effect, where likable people are perceived as having desirable personalities, as the reason likability and demographics explain part of the signal.
extraction.data: Sample of 226 public figures (N = 226) drawn from the 300 most popular figures among 11,341 in the Pantheon 1.0 dataset, across 43 countries; born 1900 or later; artists capped at 100; popularity proxied by Wikipedia page views 2008-2013; 74 figures removed for fewer than 10 raters. Human ratings from 600 Prolific raters, each rating 10 random figures on likability (200-point scale) and Big Five traits via the 10-item TIPI; mean 18.89 ratings per figure (SD 10.38). Predictors are 12,288-dimensional GPT-3 embeddings of each name. Unit of analysis: public figure. Data and code on OSF (854w2).
extraction.method: Ridge regression of mean human ratings on column-standardized GPT-3 name embeddings, with 20-fold cross-validation (each figure predicted by a model trained on all others) and alpha tuned in an inner 20-fold loop. Controlled models first regress each trait on likability plus demographics (birth year, gender) and then predict the residuals from embeddings. Correlations are corrected for attenuation by dividing by the square root of split-half reliability (0.79-0.88). Effect sizes converted to Cohen's d. Interpretation by projecting 525 person-descriptive adjectives onto the fitted regression lines.
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The design is out-of-sample predictive validity (cross-validation) with face-validity checks (top and bottom figures, adjective extremes). No causal claim is made about embeddings producing perceptions.
extraction.measures: Outcomes: mean human ratings per public figure of likability (200-point scale) and TIPI-based Big Five (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, emotional stability). Reliability: split-half reliability 0.79-0.88 used as ceiling; ICC reported in supplement. Predictors: GPT-3 name embeddings (12,288 dims). Controls: likability, birth year, gender. Popularity: log Wikipedia page views (r = 0.16 with profile similarity).
extraction.scope: Population: globally famous public figures in Pantheon 1.0 with sufficient rater coverage, born 1900 or later, from 43 countries. Era: the GPT-3 training corpus, whose date range the text does not state; the authors note predictions reflect only the training-data period. Not tested on private individuals or on people absent from the training data.
key_findings: Without controls, cross-validated predictions correlate with human ratings r = 0.78 (extraversion) to 0.88 (openness) after attenuation correction; raw r 0.70-0.80. Results p.2 and Figure 1 green bars.
Translated to Cohen's d, the no-controls correlations give d = 2.49 to 3.75 (labelled huge effects). Results p.2.

Controlling for likability and demographics, accuracy falls to r = 0.53 (emotional stability) to 0.70 (extraversion) after correction; raw r 0.43-0.61 (d = 1.25-1.96). Results p.4 and Figure 1 red bars.

Benchmarks used by authors: no-controls accuracy compared with CT detection of head and neck metastases (r = 0.64) and ultrasound for peripheral artery disease (r = 0.83); controlled accuracy compared with dental X-ray cavity detection (r = 0.43) and ultrasound for deep venous thrombosis (r = 0.60). Results p.3-4.
Self-reported Big Five from language is cited as about r = 0.40 for comparison. Results p.4.
Embeddings predict aggregate human judgments better than individual judgments do: single-rater to aggregate correlation r = 0.56-0.66. Results p.3.
Accuracy is higher for more popular figures: profile similarity correlates with log Wikipedia page views at r = 0.16. Results p.3.

Face validity: top openness figures are mostly artists (Freddie Mercury, David Bowie, Michael Jackson, Lady Gaga, Jimi Hendrix, Quentin Tarantino); bottom openness includes Kim Jong-un, Kim Jong-il and conservative politicians. Results p.3-4, Table 1.

Adjective check across 525 person-descriptive adjectives: 'quiet', 'lonely', 'depressed' sit at the low extraversion pole and 'entertaining', 'hilarious', 'lively' at the high pole; 'alcoholic' ranks 3rd (of 525) for low conscientiousness and 3rd for low emotional stability. Results p.5, Table 3.

Birth year correlates with perceived extraversion: human ratings r = 0.35 and GPT-3 predictions r = 0.44 (text, p.4; Table 2). Women are perceived as more agreeable and are absent from the bottom of predicted agreeableness. Results p.4.
Perceived personality tracks likability: many of the least likable figures (Lee Harvey Oswald, Charles Manson, both Kims) sit at undesirable extremes of several traits. Results p.4.

Discussion argues that intimate traits of public figures can be extracted from widely available LLMs, framed as a privacy threat, and that the approach could extend to people absent from training data. Discussion p.6-7; the extension is not tested in the paper.
extraction.limitations: Requires collecting human ratings to train the regression (authors suggest adjective-distance or LLM-description approaches as untested substitutes). Predictions reflect only the period in the training data, so changed public perceptions lag until retraining. Extension to people absent from the training data is untested. Sample is 226 public figures after dropping 74 with fewer than 10 raters and excluding those born before 1900; raters were Prolific workers recognising the names. Correlations concern perceived, not actual, personality. Demographic and likability controls are partial. Authors note Wikipedia-based popularity is a proxy. Supplementary materials hold the ICC and popularity details, not read here.
short_quotes: We show that people's perceptions of public figures' personalities can be accurately predicted from their names' location in GPT-3's semantic space.
Even when controlling for demographics and likability, name embeddings allow for diagnosing public figures' perceived personalities.
Our models remained accurate even when controlling for public figures' demographics and overall likability.

summary_md: Cao and Kosinski (Scientific Reports 14:6735, 2024) fit ridge regressions from 12,288-dimensional GPT-3 embeddings of public figures' NAMES to mean human ratings of perceived Big Five traits and likability (N = 226 Pantheon figures from 43 countries, 600 Prolific raters, about 19 ratings per figure, TIPI items). With 20-fold cross-validation, predictions correlate with aggregate perceptions at r = .78 to .88 after attenuation correction (raw .70 to .80). Controlling for likability and demographics (birth year, gender), accuracy falls to corrected r = .53 to .70 (raw .43 to .61). Accuracy rises with popularity (r = .16 with log Wikipedia views). The design is predictive, not causal, and concerns PERCEIVED, not actual, personality. For Melange the paper is the cited motivation for de-identifying text before the Pink LLM trait reader: a model that knows a politician's name carries a reputational prior that can stand in for reading the text. The paper shows the prior exists for famous names; it does not test whether stripping names, titles, party and states from congressional text removes it, and the repo's --named contamination probe has no output artifact in data/members. The likability result bears on the halo questions: a large evaluative factor runs through perceptions of public figures, yet trait-specific signal survives its removal, consistent with the CT-CM design of one halo method factor plus traits, and a caution that perception-based gold panels are not halo-free criteria. The code cites the work as PNAS Nexus 2024 with r = .76 to .87; the vault copy is Scientific Reports with corrected r = .78 to .88, so that citation needs checking.

related.why: Expert evaluations of senators' traits (Personality on the Hill) are a perception measure of public figures, the construct Cao and Kosinski predict from names, so reputation and halo can enter both. Cao does not cite it; the link is the analyst's.

LLM prompting for politicians' agency and communion from text. The coarse 3-point, cannot-tell-as-zero design in big5_llm.py cites Birkenmaier and Lechner. Cao does not cite it; the link is by topic and by that code citation.
Text-based measurement of elite Big Five from floor speech (Ramey, Klingler, Hollibaugh). Cao does not cite it. It marks the text route that a reputation prior must be kept separate from.

Meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five correlations, which are mostly small. Cao does not cite it, and it measures a different target (self and observer reports from text), so the rel's comparison of Cao's r with LIWC effects is not like for like.

Meta-analysis of Big Five prediction from digital footprints. Cao's about r = .40 language benchmark is cited to Park et al. 2015 (ref 39), not to this meta-analysis, so the same-method label is not supported.

Review of personality computing that lists data privacy among its threats. Cao's privacy framing (Discussion p.6) rests on Kosinski's work instead, so the two are complementary rather than sources for each other.

Politicians' Big Five personality predicts national media coverage. Cao does not test popularity against it. The perceived-personality-drives-visibility gloss is the analyst's; the excerpt read does not establish that the traits are perceived.

backlinks.why: Cao and Kosinski show that LLM-derived perceptions of public figures can be predicted from name embeddings alone (text check of the paper). That is the reputational-prior risk the de-identification step guards against, and it bears on how observer agreement is read.

meta.title: Impressive Words: Linguistic Predictors of Public Approval of the U.S. Congress

extraction.title: Impressive Words: Linguistic Predictors of Public Approval of the U.S. Congress
extraction.document_type: empirical journal article (open access, Personality and Social Psychology section)
extraction.coverage: Read full text (64,859 chars, journal pp.1-13) in four chunks: front matter, abstract, intro, methods, Tables 1-6, results, discussion, conclusion, references. Nothing skipped. No annotation files exist (annot_sha12s empty), so paul_markup is empty and none dropped. Page images not rendered. Metadata: title, authors, year, venue correct; doi was blank, filled from text. Supplement not in text file, so its numbers are not extracted.
extraction.research_question: Which demeanor makes the best impression in a professional setting: agentic (competent) language, communal (warm) language, or a specific linguistic category? Tested by predicting monthly public approval of the U.S. Congress from the words used in House floor debates, first theory-driven, then exploratory.
extraction.theory: Agency and communion as the two primary dimensions of social cognition (Bakan 1966; Fiske et al 2002; Cuddy et al 2008). Communion is split into belonging (group intimacy) and prosociality (helping others), following Frimer et al 2011. H1: agentic and communal language both positively predict approval. H2: the prosocial facet, not communion broadly, predicts approval. H3a: communal language is a stronger predictor than agentic. H3b: agentic is stronger than communal. Exploratory: all 63 LIWC categories, to find blind spots in agency/communion theory.
extraction.data: House floor-debate transcripts, Jan 1996 to Nov 2014 (Congressional Record via GPO API; extension of remarks excluded); 123,781,226 words. 22 transcripts under 5,000 words dropped; 206 monthly transcripts analysed (N = 206 months). Outcome: monthly mean of Gallup approval polls (198 of 227 months polled; gaps interpolated; mean 33%, SD 15%). Controls: President news conferences (411; 2,205,168 words); BLS unemployment; Michigan consumer sentiment; partisan vote share (mean 43%); bills passed; vetoes; female and Democratic member shares; media tone (Frimer et al 2015).
extraction.method: Word density per LIWC 2007 category (63) plus a 127-word prosocial dictionary. Five blind coders scored each category +1, 0 or -1 for agency and communion (ICC communion 0.90, agency 0.82). Indexes = z-scored densities times weights, summed. Pearson correlations; OLS Models 1 to 3 (Model 3 adds controls); z tests comparing correlations; Hayes bootstrapped mediation via media tone; exploratory stepwise regression over 63 categories (entry p < 0.005, removal p > 0.01).
extraction.identification: None. The authors state the design is correlational and cannot show that congressional language influences approval; reverse causation and third variables are acknowledged. The only strategy is adding exogenous and endogenous covariates to Model 3 (and a 6-month lag found in Frimer et al 2015, cited but not modelled here). The mediation test checks indirect paths via media tone, not causal identification.
extraction.scope: Only the U.S. House of Representatives floor speech (not the Senate, committees or extension of remarks); public approval of Congress as a whole (not individual members); monthly aggregates over 1996 to 2014.
extraction.measures: Approval: monthly average of Gallup approve or disapprove items (dichotomous). Language: LIWC 2007 densities; agency and communion indexes from coder weights; prosocial dictionary density. Media: quantity times valence of editorials (Factiva; 9-point tone). Presidential rhetoric: the same dictionaries applied to news-conference transcripts (prosocial mean 1.60 percent, SD 0.37).
key_findings: Simple correlations with approval are negative for both agency (r = -0.16, p < 0.05) and communion (r = -0.36, p < 0.001). Hypothesis 1 not supported. Table 2, p.7.
With all controls (Model 3), agency is a significant negative predictor (beta -0.11, p < 0.05) and communion is not (beta +0.04). Table 2, p.7.
Prosocial language correlates r = +0.55 (p < 0.001) with approval and stays a positive predictor with controls (beta +0.14, p < 0.05). Table 3, p.8. Supports Hypothesis 2.

Prosocial and agency correlations differ significantly (z = 7.89, p < 0.001); communion and agency also differ (z = 2.18, p = 0.03), but both are negative. The authors read this as support for Hypothesis 3b. Results, p.8.
Media tone carries indirect effects: agency B = -0.11 [-0.30, -0.02], communion -0.06 [-0.16, -0.01], prosocial +1.82 [0.17, 5.26]. Direct effects of all three are also significant. Table 4, p.8.

Moderation (text only; numbers are in the Supplement): agency predicts disapproval only when Congress is male-dominated; communal language is approved when Congress is male-dominated and disapproved otherwise; prosocial effect is stronger with fewer men and more Republicans. Results, p.8. The authors call these results mixed.

Exploratory stepwise regression keeps 8 of 63 LIWC categories. Positive: tentativeness beta 0.46, prepositions 0.41, humans 0.25, anxiety 0.24, positive emotion 0.24, numbers 0.15. Negative: second-person pronouns -0.18, conjunctions -0.26 (p < 0.005 or better). Table 5, p.8.

Media tone mediates three of the eight: prepositions indirect B = 1.90 [0.30, 5.02], humans 2.40 [0.45, 6.03], conjunctions -3.51 [-8.77, -0.45]. Not significant for tentativeness, anxiety, positive emotion, numbers or second person. Table 6, pp.9-10.
Human words correlate with prosocial words r = 0.519 (p < 0.001). Conjunction density correlates with sentence length (r = 0.24) and negatively with six-letter word density (r = -0.38). p.11.

Headline claim: prosocial (helping) language predicts approval more strongly than agentic language, which the authors read as warmth outweighing competence even in a professional setting. Abstract; Discussion, p.9.
limitations: Correlational design: no causal inference. Reverse causation is raised (for example members bonding more when approval falls). Discussion, pp.9-10.
Third variables: only the listed controls are used. Political orientation, public age and gender are not controlled, and unidentified variables may suppress an agency effect. p.10.
Approval is dichotomous (approve or disapprove), which may miss variation. p.3.
Gallup coverage is 198 of 227 months; the rest are linearly interpolated. p.3.
Agency and communion weights come from five coders at category level; robustness is claimed only in the Supplement. p.3.
No belonging dictionary was built, so the belonging-versus-helping split is tested only with Hart et al 2011 dictionaries, in the Supplement. p.10.
The 63-category stepwise analysis is exploratory with no out-of-sample test; the authors say each result is merely suggestive until replicated. p.10.
Conjunction and sentence-complexity results are described as inconclusive. p.11.
Count inconsistency: 22 excluded plus 206 retained is 228 transcripts, but the text says 227 months. Flagged, not resolved. pp.2-3.
Only the House is analysed; no Senate data; the window ends in November 2014.
Hypothesis 3 comparisons involve two negative correlations, which the authors acknowledge complicates the reading. p.8.
short_quotes: We found that neither agentic nor communal language positively predicted public approval.
To be clear, our approach is correlational, precluding the possibility of causal inference.
The American public approved of Congress more when its members spoke about helping, but not when they spoke about belonging.

summary_md: Decter-Frain and Frimer (Frontiers in Psychology 2016) ask whether the language spoken on the House floor tracks public approval of Congress. They built a monthly series from January 1996 to November 2014 (N = 206 months, about 124 million words) and scored it with LIWC 2007. Agency and communion indexes come from five coders who weighted each category (ICC 0.82 and 0.90). A separate 127-word prosocial (helping) dictionary is scored alongside them. The outcome is monthly Gallup approval. Both broad indexes correlate negatively with approval: agency r = -0.16 and communion r = -0.36. With controls, agency stays negative (beta -0.11) and communion is null. Prosocial language correlates r = +0.55 and survives the controls (beta +0.14). Media tone partly mediates all three. An exploratory stepwise pass keeps 8 of 63 categories, and the authors call these only suggestive. Moderation by the gender and party make-up of the chamber flips some signs. The design is correlational, aggregate and chamber-level, and the authors rule out causal claims. For Paul's systems the sharpest point is about construct definition. Communion is not one thing. The helping facet and the broader communion or belonging facet behave in opposite directions against an audience-perception outcome. Melange's persona channel uses one communion share from an LLM cue codebook (empathy and compassion), and that share feeds receptivity at PERSONA_W 0.30. That codebook already sits close to the helping facet, which is reassuring. But the paper's outcome is public approval of the institution, not a member's openness to lobbying, so it neither validates nor undercuts the susceptibility mapping. It also offers a cheap dictionary-based second path for checking the LLM cue shares.

bearings.paper_claim: Broad communion correlates r = -0.36 with monthly Gallup approval (Model 3 beta +0.04, n.s.) while the prosocial helping facet correlates r = +0.55 (Model 3 beta +0.14, p < 0.05). extraction.title: Advancing the Empirical Research on Lobbying
extraction.document_type: NBER working paper; narrative review essay (not peer reviewed)
extraction.coverage: Read the full text file (1346 lines, including references) in 2 chunks, lines 1-834 and 835-1346. No annotation files exist for this item (annot_sha12s empty, n_annots 0), so paul_markup is empty and 0 items were dropped. p.note absent, so this is not one of Paul research notes. Page refs are printed folio numbers. Page images not used. Metadata hints checked: title, authors, year and venue are correct; no DOI appears in the text, so doi is blank.
extraction.research_question: What empirical facts about lobbying are broadly agreed, what challenges block causal inference on lobbying effects, which quasi-experimental and structural methods can overcome them, and which data sources and open questions should drive the next generation of research (essay has no original estimates).
extraction.theory: Informational lobbying: lobbying is the transfer of information in private meetings between interest groups and politicians; politicians maximize re-election, promotion and ideological goals (p.4). Hannan-Freeman-Carroll population ecology (legitimation and competition) for counts of interest groups (pp.8-9). Expertise versus connections (who you know vs what you know) (pp.9-10). Counteractive lobbying (Austen-Smith and Wright) versus legislative subsidy (Hall and Deardorff) for targeting (p.11). Calls for empirical testing of formal models (EITM) (p.40).
extraction.data: No sample of its own. Cited studies: Blanes i Vidal et al (2012) former congressional staffers who are contract lobbyists, 22 periods (pp.18-19); de Figueiredo and Silverman (2006) university earmarks 1997-1999 (pp.22-24); Richter et al (2009) public firms, tax rates, about 10 percent lobby (pp.24-26); de Figueiredo and Cameron (2012) 38 US states (p.8); Baumgartner et al (2009) 98 issues, 2,200 advocates (p.13); Kang (2012) energy groups (p.27); Jayachandran (2006) stock returns, 2001 Jeffords switch (pp.20-21).
extraction.method: Narrative review and methods primer. Surveys the empirical facts on who lobbies, how much, and how it is organized (Sec II), then reviews five designs: difference-in-differences with exogenous shocks, event studies, instrumental variables (2SLS), two-step Heckman selection models, and structural modeling (Sec III.B). Also lists matching, regression discontinuity and synthetic control as untried for lobbying (p.29). Compares data classes: surveys, registries, transaction reports (Sec IV).
extraction.identification: Difference-in-differences: politician exits (retirement or defeat) as exogenous shock to lobbyist revenue, with lobbyist and party-chamber-time fixed effects. Event study: Jeffords party switch as shock to firm abnormal returns. IV: university overhead rates as cost shifter instrument for lobbying, excluded from earmark equation. Selection: probit selection equation with liquid assets as excluded variable, inverse Mills ratio added to tax equation. Structural: all-pay contest model estimated on policy votes.
extraction.measures: Lobbying expenditures from federal LDA and state transaction reports; counts of registered groups and lobbyists; lobbyist revenue; effective tax rates; earmark dollars; abnormal stock returns; soft money as party alignment; overhead rates as instrument; liquid assets as selection variable; inverse Mills ratio.
extraction.scope: Mostly US federal and state lobbying (LDA federal data, US state transaction data), with brief mention of Japan, China, India, Mexico, Norway and other developed or transition economies (p.35-36). Literature reviewed through 2013; federal disclosure under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995 (p.34). Excludes campaign finance, illegal lobbying and bribery, and bureaucratic lobbying (footnote 1, p.4).
key_findings: Federal lobbying spending was about 3.5 billion dollars in 2012, against roughly 750 million a year in interest-group campaign contributions, about five times as large (Sec II.A, pp.5-6).
Corporations and trade associations account for over 84 percent of federal lobbying expenditures; issue-ideology membership groups about 2 percent (de Figueiredo 2004 as cited, Sec II.A, p.6).

Only about 10 percent of publicly traded firms lobby on their own behalf (Richter et al 2009; Kerr et al 2013); a firm lobbying last year lobbies this year with 92 percent probability (Sec II.A, p.7).
Budgeting periods are associated with a 19 percent increase in state interest-group lobbying expenditures across 38 states (de Figueiredo 2014; de Figueiredo and Cameron 2012) (Sec II.A, p.8).

Lobbyist revenue falls about 23 percent after the senator they formerly served is defeated or retires (Blanes i Vidal et al 2012) (Sec II.C, p.10); the essay attributes about 23 percent of lobbying services value to who you know (Sec III.B.1, p.20).

Richter et al (2009): a 1 percent increase in lobbying over baseline predicts a 1.07 percentage point lower effective tax rate in the next period, and the result survives a Heckman selection correction (Sec III.B.4, p.26).
de Figueiredo and Silverman (2006): lobbying raises earmarks only when the district legislator sits on an appropriations committee; no significant effect otherwise (Sec III.B.3, p.24).
Kang (2012) structural all-pay contest: expenditure effects on enactment are very small, but the marginal return in policy is about 140 percent (Sec III.B.5, p.28).
Jayachandran (2006): firms more aligned with the former Republican majority lost market value after the Jeffords switch (Sec III.B.2, p.21).
Baumgartner et al (2009): across 98 issues, both sides mobilize roughly equal resources; policies are stable and change, when it occurs, is substantial (Sec II.D, p.13).
Targeting: powerful, allied and marginal legislators are lobbied; staunch enemies are not. Counteractive and subsidy accounts give different predictions (Sec II.C, pp.10-11).
State interest-group counts follow an inverted-U over time from legitimation then competition, and rise with economy size and number of issues (Sec II.B, pp.8-9).
limitations: Essay itself reports no new estimates; its consensus claims are a synthesis of cited work (p.2-3, Sec II).
Lobbying panels show persistence and little within-group variation, so fixed effects need external shocks (Sec III.A, p.16).
Omitted variables are pervasive because some instruments of influence are unobserved (p.16-17).
Endogenous selection into lobbying is not random; about 10 percent of interests lobby, so returns may be biased upward (p.17).

Difference-in-differences can have inconsistent standard errors; event windows can be confounded; weak instruments and small selection samples can doom IV and selection models; structural assumptions may be unbelievable (footnote 3, p.28).
Survey data suffers from non-response, non-random samples, recall error and little verifiability (p.32).
Registries count groups, include zero-spend registrants, and mix rules across jurisdictions (p.33).
Transaction data gives spending and intensity but not message content and not which legislator was targeted (pp.34-35).
Outcome variables are often weakly linked to lobbying; authors call for institutional detail on the link (p.30).

summary_md: De Figueiredo and Richter (NBER WP 19698, 2013) is a narrative review with no new estimates. It sets out what the field agreed on about lobbying by 2013 and how to study it causally. The scale facts: federal lobbying was about 3.5 billion dollars in 2012, roughly five times interest-group campaign contributions. Corporations and trade associations account for over 84 percent of it. Only about 10 percent of public firms lobby, and a firm that lobbied last year lobbies this year with 92 percent probability. Its main argument is that lobbying panels are persistent, selected and confounded by unobserved channels. Fixed effects alone therefore cannot identify effects, and research should use exogenous shocks. The designs it reviews are difference-in-differences on legislator exits, event studies such as the Jeffords switch, cost-shifter instruments, Heckman selection, and structural all-pay contest models. It cites conditional returns: earmark gains only where the home legislator sits on Appropriations, a 1.07 percentage point lower tax rate per 1 percent more lobbying, and about 23 percent of lobbyist revenue lost when a former boss leaves office. It also notes that transaction (LDA) data record spending but not which legislator was targeted. For Paul's systems the essay mostly confirms choices already made. It agrees that the lobbied-member link is circular (LD-2 names no member) and explains why the sector-growth lobbying coefficient flips under year fixed effects. It also shows that the influence engine's money legs cover only PAC contributions, the smaller channel. Its shock-based designs point to tests the system has not run. Nothing in it argues for either rejected SNA proposal. Its revolving-door evidence must not be turned into influence language on staffer edges.

extraction.venue: MPRA Paper 87612, Munich Personal RePEc Archive (posted 02 Jul 2018; dated June 2018)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in one pass (72,168 chars, 1,309 lines): front matter, abstract, introduction, conceptual framework, data, all results sections (4.1-4.3), conclusion, references, Tables 1-6, Figures 1-3 (text labels only; page images not rendered), and Appendix A (dataset construction, matching) and B (Table 7, RD placebo figures 4-6). Metadata hint corrected: co-author is Brian Kelleher Richter. Annotations: p.annot_sha12s is empty and no _annots file matches sha12 0dc33fec3429, so paul_markup is empty (0 items; 0 dropped). p.note is not set, so this is not one of Paul's own notes. Topic coverage: lobbying yes; allocation yes; elections yes; legislators only indirectly (candidate-level giving); networks no; path-finding no; persuasion or turnout no; text measurement no. Table 3 column alignment is ambiguous in the text extraction; column numbers follow the paper's own prose.
extraction.research_question: Do statutory limits on corporate PAC campaign contributions generate spillover increases in other corporate political activity, namely CEO contributions to the same candidates and firm lobbying expenditures, at the regulated per-candidate contribution threshold?
extraction.theory: Revealed-preference firm model (Section 2, pp.5-7): firms give to candidates until marginal benefit equals the dollar; a binding per-candidate cap creates a positive shadow price, so firms substitute toward other channels. Lobbying is also read as a legislative subsidy (Hall and Deardorff 2006) and as a possible cost of access. The authors state the design is theory-agnostic and is not a test of theories of firm political behavior (p.4).
extraction.data: S&P 500 firms present at any point 1991-2008; 950 firms in contribution data. Contributions: FEC filings via Center for Responsive Politics bulk data; CEO identity and firm characteristics from COMPUSTAT/ExecuComp; PAC-to-firm mapping from Myers (2005). Unit for PAC and CEO models: firm-candidate-cycle, 6,803,661 observations over nine federal cycles, 1992-2008. Lobbying: LDA disclosures for engagements over 10,000 dollars, 2000-2008, firm-cycle unit; 2,796 firm-cycle observations stated in Section 3 (p.8); regression samples 2,783 observations and 787 firms (Table 3, p.29), 1,908 observations and 579 lobbying firms (Table 3 columns 4-6), 4,821 observations and 943 firms (placebos, Table 4), 2,200 or 2,191 observations and 700 or 693 firms (RD, Table 5).
extraction.method: Linear probability and OLS. CEO model (eq. 3, p.10): binary CEO-to-candidate contribution on PAC contributed and PAC at-limit indicators with firm-by-cycle and candidate-by-cycle fixed effects. Lobbying model (eq. 4, p.13): firm-cycle aggregate lobbying on PAC contributed and at-limit indicators with firm fixed effects and Fama-French 49 industry-by-cycle fixed effects. One-sided regression discontinuity (eq. 5, p.16): polynomial (linear or quadratic) in PAC dollars with a jump at the limit, with and without industry-cycle fixed effects. Difference-in-differences around BCRA (post-2003 cycle indicator, Table 6, p.18). Standard errors clustered by firm. Altonji, Elder and Taber (2005) selection-on-unobservables ratio reported for the main lobbying model (p.14).
extraction.identification: CEO model: within firm-cycle, cross-candidate variation across the statutory per-candidate limit, assuming firm-by-candidate-by-cycle factors are orthogonal to CEO giving (p.4). Lobbying model: firm and industry-cycle fixed effects, plus assumed smoothness of lobbying absent regulation, which the authors test on advertising, R&D and dividends in the appendix (p.4-5, p.A-4 to A-7). RD: assumes optimization frictions so firms cannot perfectly control PAC dollars around the limit; authors call this strong (p.17). BCRA 2002 soft-money ban is the only exogenous policy change; it leaves PAC limits intact. The authors say there is no exogenous variation in FEC limits, so results are partial correlations (p.14).
extraction.scope: US federal elections; large publicly traded S&P 500 firms with PACs; contributions 1992-2008; lobbying 2000-2008, so only a single pre-BCRA lobbying cycle. Excludes state politics, super PACs (post-window), independent expenditures and in-kind or philanthropic channels (pp.19-20).
key_findings: CEO supplementary giving (Table 2, p.28): at-limit PAC raises the probability a CEO gives to that candidate by 0.066 (SE 0.006). The text instead reports 7.7 percent (Section 4.1, p.11), a mismatch noted here.

CEO dollars (Table 2, p.28): at-limit PAC associated with 109.92 extra dollars (SE 10.05). Text reports 123 dollars (p.11); Table 7 (p.A-4) gives 123.88 (SE 10.55). Figure 2 shows 59.91 for the 4,500-4,999 bin versus the at-limit value.

Lobbying main estimate (Table 3 column 1, p.29; text p.14): firms whose PAC reaches the limit for any candidate spend 549,166 dollars more per cycle (SE 225,013; significant at 1 percent). Abstract gives a range of 549,000 to 1.6M dollars.
Lobbying firms only (Table 3 column 6, p.29; text p.15): at-limit coefficient 662,590 dollars (SE 305,066; significant at 5 percent).

Large-expenditure control (Table 3 columns 2-3, p.14-15): PAC-large-expenditure indicator is not significant; at-limit remains significant when both are included, about 250,000 dollars larger than the large-expenditure coefficient per text. Altonji-Elder-Taber ratio stated as 7.7 (p.14).

Placebo outcomes (Table 4, p.30; text p.15): at-limit coefficients are R&D 63.07 (SE 68.56), advertising 4.71 (SE 34.74), dividends -23.02 (SE 66.93), acquisitions 5.32 (SE 103.31); none significant. Units not stated in the paper.

One-sided RD on lobbying (Table 5, p.30; text pp.16-17): jump of 3,001,984 (linear, no industry-cycle FE), 2,427,612 (quadratic), 2,250,564 (linear, industry-cycle FE) and 1,630,744 (quadratic, industry-cycle FE), all significant at 1 percent. Figure 3 (p.26) plots the discontinuity.

BCRA difference-in-differences on lobbying (Table 6, p.31): at-limit times post-BCRA coefficient 539,008.1 (SE 220,949.6), significant at 1 percent. Text reports a 145 percent increase (p.18), with a caveat about the single pre-BCRA lobbying cycle.

BCRA on CEO giving (Table 6, p.31): at-limit times post-BCRA coefficient 16.54 (SE 11.77), not significant. Text reports a 16 percent increase (p.18), which does not match the dollar units of the table.

Descriptives (Table 1, p.27; text p.8): average PAC contribution to all candidates 68.48 dollars (SD 553.79); 2,266.53 among recipients; 14.4 percent of recipients receive the maximum. CEO average 2.00 overall and 1,323.98 among recipients. Mean lobbying 1,101,868 dollars for all firms and 2,898,788 for lobbying firms.

Authors' summary (Section 1, pp.3-5; Conclusion, p.19): statutory limits on corporate PACs are effectively non-binding, and spillovers into lobbying can exceed the contribution limit by more than 100 times.
Smoothness and placebo figures (Appendix B, Figures 4-6, pp.A-5 to A-7): advertising, R&D and tax-expenditure outcomes show no comparable jump at the PAC limit, supporting the smoothness assumption.
limitations: No exogenous variation in FEC limits; estimates are partial correlations (p.14).
Lobbying is observed at firm-cycle level, so the at-limit indicator is coarser and identifying variation is reduced (Section 4.2, p.13).
RD needs optimization frictions so firms cannot perfectly control PAC dollars; the authors call this assumption strong (p.17).
CEO estimates are a lower bound because only CEOs are studied; other managers may also give (p.11).
LDA filings do not name candidates, so firm-candidate lobbying cannot be linked; the mapping rests on an approximation with a stepwise function (A.3-A.4, pp.A-1 to A-3).
Only one pre-BCRA lobbying cycle; the authors caution against over-interpreting the BCRA results (p.18).
Theory-agnostic design; no welfare or optimal-regulation counterfactual (pp.6, 19).
Excludes state politics, super PACs and independent expenditures outside the window (pp.19-20).
Reverse causality and joint determination of lobbying and at-limit giving acknowledged; firm and industry-cycle fixed effects mitigate but do not remove it (pp.13-14).

Internal inconsistencies between text and tables: CEO probability 7.7 percent versus 0.066 in Table 2; CEO dollars 123 versus 109.92; BCRA CEO 16 percent versus a dollar coefficient; Table 3 column labels in the prose do not match the printed layout.

summary_md: Fremeth, Richter and Schaufele (MPRA working paper, 2018) ask whether the federal per-candidate cap on corporate PAC gifts (5,000 dollars per election, 10,000 per cycle) pushes firms into other political channels. They use S&P 500 firms with PACs, 1992-2008 FEC data (6.8M firm-candidate-cycle rows) and LDA lobbying for 2000-2008 (about 2,800 firm-cycles). Within a firm-cycle, a candidate who receives the PAC maximum is 6.6 points more likely to also receive a gift from the firm's CEO (Table 2), about 110 dollars more on average. Firms whose PAC maxes out any candidate spend about 549,000 dollars more on lobbying per cycle, with firm and industry-by-cycle fixed effects. A one-sided regression discontinuity at the limit gives jumps of 1.6M to 3.0M dollars, but the authors call its frictions assumption strong. Placebo outcomes (R&D, advertising, dividends, acquisitions) show no jump. The authors say no exogenous variation in the limit exists, so the estimates are partial correlations. Some numbers in the text do not match the tables. For Paul's systems, the paper bears mainly on how money is bounded. The Melange optimizer treats the 10,000-dollar PAC limit as the ceiling on CU spend per member, and the flip model counts competitor money only as bank and finserv PAC dollars. The paper suggests firms at the cap shift resources into executive giving and lobbying, which neither ledger sees. Mentat already tiers Chief-level employee giving by company, so a PAC-at-limit by Chief-giving join is a cheap extension. The paper's firm-level link between giving and lobbying does not contradict the member-level FEC-LDA bridge null. That bridge asks a different question, and the paper itself notes that LDA filings name no candidates.

The summary and bearing 1 say limits are non-binding on total corporate political activity. The paper says corporate PAC limits are effectively non-binding and that spillovers can be economically meaningful.

No firm-level version of the FEC-LDA bridge (an organization's giving against the same organization's LDA spend) has been specified. All bridge rounds were member-level.

The paper's text and tables disagree: CEO probability is 7.7 percent in the text vs 0.066 in Table 2, CEO dollars 123 vs 109.92, and the BCRA CEO effect is reported as 16 percent against a dollar coefficient. Cite the table values.

extraction.research_question: Why does bipartisanship persist in Congress despite polarization and primary threats? The paper asks whether legislators who attract a larger share of opposite-party cosponsors on their bills are more effective at advancing them, whether that holds across eras and party conditions, whether the effect has an optimum, and whether offering bipartisan cosponsorships in turn drives attracting them (reciprocity).
extraction.data: Sample: all Representatives and Senators serving in the 93rd-114th Congresses (1973-2016); independents excluded. Unit: legislator by two-year Congress. Bills: all public bills introduced in the period. Cosponsorship data for 93rd-110th Congresses from Fowler (2006), updated by the authors for 111th-114th. N: House 8,997 to 9,202 legislator-Congress observations; Senate 2,167 to 2,192 (Table 1). Hitchhiker law sample (Table A11): 4,494 House observations, 1993-2014.
extraction.method: Cross-sectional time-series least squares regressions with legislator fixed effects and robust standard errors (Tables 1-3, A2-A13); pooled OLS and fixed-effects OLS for reciprocity regressions (Table 4, clustered SEs in pooled models). Nonlinear models add a squared term. Robustness: commemorative-bill exclusion, normalization by Congress, cosponsorship-level controls, low-cosponsorship eras, binary alternative measures, Lugar index, no member FE, electoral safety interactions, later legislative stages, hitchhiker-inclusive law counts, and era splits (pre/post 1994).
extraction.scope: US Congress, House and Senate, 1973-2016, public bills only. Population is all members in that window. The argument concerns individual lawmaking effectiveness, not chamber-level outcomes; the 60-vote cloture environment is offered to explain higher Senate levels.
key_findings: Table 1 Model 1.2 (House, p.17): proportion bipartisan cosponsors attracted = 0.433 (SE 0.097), p<0.001; Model 1.5 (Senate, p.17) = 0.330 (SE 0.147), p<0.05. One SD increase = +0.08 LES in House and +0.06 in Senate, about 6-8 percent of mean LES of 1.0 (p.16).

Uncontrolled Models 1.1 (House 0.986) and 1.4 (Senate 0.538) are larger; the coefficient on proportion bipartisan cosponsorships offered is not significant with controls (Model 1.3 = -0.234; Model 1.6 = -0.420) (p.17-18).
Robust to excluding commemorative bills, normalizing by Congress, controlling for cosponsorship levels, binary alternative measures (Table A5 House 0.213, p<0.001) and the Lugar index (p.18-19).
Without member fixed effects coefficients are larger (Table A6 with controls: House 0.552, p<0.001; Senate 0.440, p<0.001) (p.18-19, Appendix p.10).

Table 2 (p.20-21): effect stays positive and significant (House 0.432 to 0.629; Senate 0.358 to 0.442) when interacted with a Congress counter, majority margin or party polarization; all interactions small and not significant.

Table 3 nonlinearity (p.22-23): House linear 1.828 and squared -1.844 peak at 0.496; Senate 1.666 and -1.626 peak at 0.512. A one-SD decline costs about 22 percent of LES in House and 16 percent in Senate; a one-SD rise adds about 8 and 4 percent (p.24).

Majority and minority subsamples show similar nonlinear shapes (Table 3 Models 3.2-3.3, 3.5-3.6). Authors read the larger majority coefficients as a scale artifact, since majority LES is about three times minority LES (p.24-25).
Reciprocity (Table 4, p.27): offering bipartisan cosponsorships predicts attracting them. House pooled 0.626 (SE 0.039); House with member FE 0.317; Senate pooled 0.739; Senate FE 0.547; all p<0.001.
Distance from median predicts fewer bipartisan cosponsors in pooled models (House -0.154, Senate -0.114) but the House effect disappears with member FE (0.005) (p.27).

Later stages (Table A8, House, Appendix p.12): bipartisan share predicts action in committee 0.894, beyond committee 0.853, passing chamber 0.800, and becoming law 0.485 (all p<0.001). Senate committee-stage model A9.2 is not significant (1.767); Senate law model A9.5 = 0.589 (p<0.05) (Appendix p.13).

Law production (Table A10, Appendix p.14): nonlinear House laws 1.685 with squared -1.586; Senate 2.342 with squared -2.135; output rises to about 50 percent bipartisan cosponsors and falls after. Hitchhiker-inclusive laws 1993-2014 (Table A11): linear 0.691, p<0.001.

Eras and electoral safety: House effect 0.470 (1973-94) and 0.380 (1995-2016); Senate 0.332 and 0.307 (Tables A12-A13, Appendix p.16-17). Electoral-safety interaction not significant (Table A7). Descriptives (Table A1): mean share 0.290 House (SD 0.194), 0.354 Senate (SD 0.190); median 30-40 percent in the 1970s-80s (Figure 1, p.12-13).
limitations: LES omits oversight, constituent service, obstruction and amendment success; authors note amendment-success research is a gap (p.8-9, footnote 5).
Cosponsorship treated as public endorsement; the authors concede it is debatable whether it implies effort to pass the bill (p.9-10).

No design-based identification. Legislator fixed effects and controls only; time-varying confounders not excluded. Authors call the coefficient a within-member marginal impact (p.15) and mostly use associational language.
House cosponsor cap of 25 before 1979 and low early cosponsorship rates (footnote 9, p.11); addressed in robustness Table A4 only.
Table notes report one-tailed significance tests. Supplemental appendix is stated as to be posted online; the appendix tables are included in the text file.
The Table A9 note claims greater success starting with passage out of committee, but Model A9.2 (committee action) is not significant, so the note overstates the Senate committee-stage result.
short_quotes: bipartisanship unambiguously helps individual legislators who seek to advance their policy goals (abstract, p.1)
Holding the number of bill cosponsorships constant, as a legislator attracts more cosponsors from the opposite party to her bills, her value increases (p.11)
the effect of bipartisanship rises until about half of all of a member's cosponsors are from each party, and then falls again (p.22-23)
extraction.theory: Two competing hypotheses. Bipartisanship and Effectiveness: spatial models (Krehbiel 1998) imply successful bills need pivotal veto-player support; bipartisan support signals quality to gatekeepers (Koger 2003) and refines proposals (p.4-6). Partisanship and Effectiveness: leaders reward one-sided party support (Cox and McCubbins 2005; Hastert Rule), and policy specialists achieve more (Bernhard and Sulkin 2018) (p.6-7). Conditional hypotheses cover majority status, era and polarization (p.7-8). Reciprocity: offering cross-party cosponsorships generates reciprocal ones (p.25-26).
extraction.identification: No instrument, natural experiment or design-based strategy. Identification relies on legislator fixed effects (within-member variation), a standard covariate set from the effectiveness literature, and robustness checks. Authors interpret coefficients as associations and separately test the offered-vs-attracted distinction (p.15-18). Reverse causation and time-varying confounds are not formally addressed.
extraction.measures: DV: Legislative Effectiveness Score (LES; Volden and Wiseman 2014, 2018), mean 1.03 House and 1.01 Senate (Table A1). Main IV: Proportion Bipartisan Cosponsors Attracted, the mean across a member's bills with at least one cosponsor of the share of cosponsors from the other party (mean 0.29 House, 0.35 Senate). Also: Proportion Bipartisan Cosponsorships Offered; seniority; party and leadership; chairs; power committee; distance from median (DW-NOMINATE); delegation size; vote share; up for reelection (Senate); average cosponsors attracted; polarization; majority margin.

summary_md: Harbridge-Yong, Volden and Wiseman ask whether bipartisanship pays for individual lawmakers. They use all House and Senate members in the 93rd-114th Congresses (1973-2016; about 9,000 House and 2,170 Senate legislator-Congress rows) and regress the Volden-Wiseman Legislative Effectiveness Score on the share of a member's cosponsors who come from the other party. The design uses legislator fixed effects. That attracted share predicts effectiveness: within member, the coefficient is 0.433 in the House and 0.330 in the Senate, so one SD is worth about 6-8 percent of mean LES. The share members offer to the other party's bills does not predict effectiveness once controls are in. The effect holds across eras, majority margins and polarization levels, and in majority and minority strata. It is an inverted U that peaks near a 50/50 cosponsor mix (0.496 House, 0.512 Senate). In the House the attracted share also predicts each later stage, from committee action to law. Offering cross-party cosponsorships predicts attracting them, at 0.317 within member in the House and 0.547 in the Senate. The evidence is observational, with one-tailed tests and no design-based identification. For Paul's system, the sharpest point concerns direction. bpf is an undirected, symmetrized cross-party tie share. Cooperation v2's directional component measures offered support. Nothing in the system measures attracted support, which is the side the paper ties to effectiveness. The flip model's (1+0.3 bpf) passage bonus and the coalition seed boost (1+0.8 bpf) are monotone, but the paper finds a peak and then a decline. The paper's reciprocity is cosponsorship exchange. It does not validate the money reciprocity in D-104..D-108. Any transfer is UNVERIFIED until it is reproduced on Paul's data.

bearings.system_side: bpf() in fec/moneyball_core.py reads bipartisan.json (default 0.24). The materialize script builds that file: each undirected pair takes the mean of its two directed rows when both directions exist, otherwise the single directed weight; member share = (cross + 6 x prior) / (same + cross + 6). summary_issues: bpf symmetrization: the rel says every pair takes the mean of its two directed weights; the code uses the single directed weight when only one direction exists.
Offered and attracted ties cannot be recovered: overstated. The materialize output keeps source_directed_weights, so an attracted share is buildable from data on disk but is not built.
Later-stage effects: the Table A8-A9 DVs are counts of a member's bills at each stage, not stage rates, and not LES. The rel line that the LES outcome is the CEL score mislabels them.
Shadow checked against CEL LES: not found in the code read; treat as unsupported.
Majority/minority similar shapes: holds for the House. The Senate minority squared term (Model 3.6, -0.397) is not significant, so the Senate minority shape is not established.
Reciprocity halving: House pooled 0.626 to FE 0.317 roughly halves; Senate 0.739 to 0.547 does not. The rho .888 sentence is a non sequitur for the paper link.

Flip-model card: the claim that the component card says the code has no bonus was not checked, since the card text was not available. The 8-14 percent attribution to Volden-Wiseman is not in this paper.
Senate Table A9 note overstates the committee-stage result (A9.2 1.767 not significant). Confirmed as the rel flags.

gaps_exposed: No ATTRACTED-direction bipartisan share exists anywhere in the system. bpf is undirected and symmetrized, and cooperation v2 c2 measures offered support. The paper ties only the attracted share to effectiveness.
Every bpf consumer is monotone: the flip passage bonus (1+0.3 bpf) and the coalition seed boost (1+0.8 bpf). The paper finds an inverted U peaking near a 0.5 share in both chambers.

The flip-model comment cites a Volden-Wiseman bonus of +8-14 percent, but this paper reports 6-8 percent of mean LES per SD. The component card says the code line has no bonus, yet flip_model.py:142 carries (1+0.3*bpf), so the card is stale.
bpf is a single current-roster snapshot. The paper's effects are within member across Congresses, and the system has no per-Congress bipartisan series to test them.
The effectiveness shadow has never been checked against bipartisan coalition composition, which is a ready convergent-validity test against CEL LES.
flags: The paper's reciprocity is cosponsorship exchange between members. It does not validate the money or competitiveness reciprocity in D-104..D-108, which stays NOT validated. Do not cite this paper for it.
The paper controls for average cosponsors attracted in its regressions. That is not per-edge volume normalization and gives no support to the rejected per-edge normalization proposal.

The evidence is observational with legislator FE and one-tailed tests, and it has no design-based identification, so it supports associational language only. The Table A9 note overstates the Senate committee-stage result (A9.2 is not significant).
Coefficients are reported by chamber and by majority/minority strata. Quote them by chamber with the 1973-2016 window, never as one pooled number.
bpf and any attracted-share variant are heuristic model outputs, not closeness or access probabilities (D-025).
Transfer of any of these effects to Paul's current-roster data is UNVERIFIED until reproduced by a second path (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotated entry for this work. The evidence agrees in direction with his bpf position, which cites Bacik on bipartisan teams earning more, and with his choice of LES as the effectiveness criterion for the shadow lane. It refines rather than contradicts both. The payoff is to bipartisan support attracted, not offered, and it is nonlinear. No Paul note is stale because of this paper. The flip-model comment and the component card describing it are out of step with the code and with the paper's magnitudes.

related.why: Sotoudeh (2024) measures cosponsorship influence on House bill passage and contrasts it with the Volden-Wiseman LES. This paper uses LES as its outcome.
Battaglini, Leone Sciabolazza and Patacchini model LES as a Katz-Bonacich centrality of the cosponsorship network. This paper uses the cross-party composition of cosponsors instead.
Bucchianeri, Volden and Wiseman extend the Volden-Wiseman effectiveness framework to American state legislatures (SLES).
Aroyehun (2026) also regresses Congressional LES on a member-level predictor, emotional expression from floor speeches. The link is a shared outcome, not shared data.

Aref and Neal (2021) partition House cosponsorship signed networks; their third coalition, marked by negative same-party ties, is the most effective coalition in most sessions. Their coalitions are signed-network partitions, not cross-party by definition.
